title: Design strategies and elements of building envelope for urban acoustic environment
review_question: To conduct a systematic review of building design elements for better urban acoustic environment based on previous acoustical studies, and to derive building envelope design strategies from the building envelope design elements.
inclusion_exclusion_criteria: Studies published from 1970 to February 2020, identified through ScienceDirect, Scopus, ProQuest Central, Web of Science, and American Institute of Physics. Included articles must be related to acoustics, built environment, and outdoor acoustics, with information on urban morphology and outdoor acoustics improvement. Excluded studies lacked information on noise abatement, soundscape aspects, or objective measurements.

synthesis_conclusions: Geometric and material building envelope design elements can effectively reduce outdoor noise levels.
Vegetation on building envelopes demonstrates good performance in both noise abatement and soundscape improvement.
Four key design strategies for building envelopes are identified: textured/fragmented surfaces, increased sound absorption, multisensory design, and integrated design.
Multisensory design, incorporating visual, olfactory, and thermal factors, can enhance soundscape perception and overall human environmental perception.
An integrated design process involving architects, acousticians, and urban planners is crucial for achieving a good urban acoustic environment.
evidence_gaps: Acoustic studies lack sufficient supportive results and practical applications to be appropriately reflected in architectural design beyond the acoustic field.
The insertion loss of individual design elements could not be quantified individually due to the combined effects of test conditions.
Multisensory interaction on acoustic environmental perception has not been comprehensively investigated.
Research on aircraft, railway, or wind turbine noise is limited, preventing conclusive findings for these sources.
heterogeneity_sources: Differences in noise levels definitions (noise reduction, level differences, noise attenuation, insertion loss)
Variations in test conditions and combinations of design elements across studies

moderators.effect: Insertion loss varies significantly by noise type (road traffic, aircraft, railway, wind turbine, unspecified).
moderators.subgroup_effects: Road traffic and unspecified noise showed moderate reduction, while aircraft, railway, and wind turbine showed varied but generally weaker effects due to low study count.

moderators.effect: Insertion loss varies by measurement/prediction method.
moderators.subgroup_effects: Prediction and scale-model measurements showed higher insertion loss compared to field and laboratory measurements.

moderators.effect: Insertion loss varies depending on whether the receiver is in a directly exposed canyon, shielded canyon, or courtyard.
moderators.subgroup_effects: Shielded canyons and courtyards generally showed higher insertion loss than directly exposed canyons.

moderators.effect: Insertion loss varies by the primary research approach.
moderators.subgroup_effects: Both geometry/material and vegetation approaches showed comparable noise reduction effects, with vegetation showing slightly higher insertion loss for unspecified noise.

limitations: The number of studies for aircraft, railway, and wind turbine noise was small, limiting conclusive findings.
The quantitative synthesis for subgroups (e.g., receiver's location, research approach) did not always provide explicit 'k' values for each subgroup.
Discrepancies between numerical values stated in the text and those visually represented in figures for some noise types (e.g., aircraft, railway, wind turbine insertion loss).
